cb2587a3743ace0be5fb3e156470a93a.title: How do you say ibuprofen? (Pronunciation Series Episode 80)
cb2587a3743ace0be5fb3e156470a93a.description: A small substitution can make a big difference to your ear. The official pronunciation for ibuprofen is EYE-bue-PROE-fen. Notice the second syllable, "bue." I have been saying "bee" instead of "bue" for decades. I first became aware of the official pronunciation in 2020, when I looked it up in the USP Dictionary Online. The way I say it is "in the ballpark." It's close enough, but it's not technically correct. As I recorded this episode, I felt uncomfortable admitting my decades-long mistake and owning the fact that I choose to say ibuprofen wrong even though I know better. I just feel more comfortable saying EYE-bee-PROE-fen. A lot of people say EYE-bee-PROE-fen instead of EYE-bue-PROE-fen. That doesn't make it right, but I'm happy to say that both variations sound about the same when said quickly. Pick your pronunciation, and own it when you say it! This is the 80th episode in my drug pronunciation series. We talk about pronunciations, not pharmacology. If you want to feel less frustrated learning drug names and sound more confident saying them, follow this series. Ibuprofen = EYE-bue-PROE-fen EYE, like eyeglasses bue, like butane (My variation is "bee," like a bumblebee.") PROE, like a the abbreviation for "professional." For example, Caitlin Clark is a pro American women's basketball player in the WNBA fen, which rhymes with ten Emphasize EYE and PRO. PRO gets the most emph

b863877814d58d95df9b98556373662e.description: This is the 79th episode in my drug pronunciation series. In this episode, I divide dextroamphetamine and Dexedrine into syllables, tell you which syllables to emphasize, and list my sources. We cover pronunciations, not pharmacology. If you want to feel less frustrated learning drug names and sound more confident saying them, follow this series. Dextroamphetamine = DEX-troe-am-FET-a-meen DEX, as in "dexter," the Latin word meaning "right." (Right as opposed to left.) Troe, like a Trojan Horse am, as in I am an Ohio-licensed pharmacist FET, like fetch (For example, "Jack and Jill went up the hill to fetch a pail of water.") A (uh), which is a short "A" sound, like the "A" in the word "adoption" (uh) meen, as in bullies are mean. Emphasize DEX and FET. FET gets the most emphasis. Written pronunciation source: USP Dictionary Online https://links.thepharmacistsvoice.com/uspdictionaryonline Spoken pronunciation example: Merriam Webster's Online Dictionary and Tony PharmD's YouTube Channel https://links.thepharmacistsvoice.com/tonypharmddextroamphetamine Dexedrine = dek-suh-drin dek, like a deck of cards suh, like supper drin, which rhymes with thin. In the literature, no emphasis is indicated on any syllable. I tend to emphasize "dek." 711de6ef7f553e812bc259b3801514af.title: How do you say abciximab? (Pronunciation Series Episode 74)
711de6ef7f553e812bc259b3801514af.description: This is the 74th episode in my drug pronunciation series. In this episode, I divide abciximab into syllables, tell you which syllable to emphasize, and list my sources. ❌ We don't cover pharmacology in this series. Just pronunciations. How do you say abciximab? abciximab = ab-SIX-i-mab, ab, like abdomen SIX, like the number 6 i, which is a short "I" sound, like the "I" in the word, "president" (sounds like, "ih") mab, which is the stem for monoclonal antibodies Emphasize SIX Sources: USP Dictionary Online or drugs.com When I was a hospital pharmacy intern in the 90s, I didn't know how to say abciximab. It was a relatively new drug name at the time, and I kinda spelled it out instead of saying it. I just need to hear it once. Then, I knew how to say it forevermore. Why pick abciximab for the series? Even though my sources say that abciximab (ReoPro) has been discontinued in the US, it is still discussed among healthcare professionals and mentioned in printed resources. Therefore, the pronunciation is worth knowing. You may hear someone say it during your lifetime, and this podcast episode will help you connect the printed name with the spoken name. Plus, if you spell out drug names because you don't know how to say them, you might relate to this episode. I know what it's like to feel insecure saying something I have never heard before.
